pos: n. (city on the Lake of Geneva in the Pays de Vaud; reformed after the Disputation of 1536)
etymology: From Latin Lausonium, the Roman settlement on the lake shore; later French Lausanne.
biblical_def: Lausanne was the cathedral city of the Pays de Vaud, and the Reformation came to it by argument. In October 1536 the Bernese magistrates convened a public disputation there; William Farel and Pierre Viret led the evangelical side, and a young Frenchman lately arrived in the country, John Calvin, rose to answer the charge that the Reformers had despised the ancient church, and answered it out of the fathers from memory. The city went over to the Reformation, the mass was abolished, and in 1537 an academy was founded which for two decades was the chief school of French-speaking Protestantism; Viret taught there for twenty-two years, Theodore Beza held the Greek chair, and the men trained in its halls carried the Reformed faith back into France. The dictionary records Lausanne because it is the clearest case in the whole Reformation of a city turning on a public, documented, answerable argument from Scripture rather than on a prince's decree. That is the apostolic pattern: Paul “three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2), and Apollos “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disputation as reasoning in opposition to something, doctrine as that which is taught and held forth as true, and academy as a seminary of learning between the university and the common school.
webster_full: DISPUTATION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something.
DOCTRINE, n. Principles or positions in any science; whatever is taught; that which is held, put forth as true, and supported by a teacher.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college, and a common school.
REA'SON, n. A faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, and good from evil.
scriptures: Act 17:2
And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures,
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: A cathedral city reformed by public disputation in 1536, and an academy that trained the French Reformed ministry for twenty years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern assumption that public religious argument is bad manners, so that doctrine is settled by sentiment, institutional momentum, or the unexamined confidence of whoever holds the chair. Lausanne settled it the other way: both sides stated their case in the hearing of the city, from texts the city could check.

The principle to recover is that the truth of God bears examination and asks for it. The apostolic manner was argument out of the text: Paul “three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2), and Apollos “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly” (Act 18:28). A minister is required to be equal to it — “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — and the whole church is charged to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

“shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28) — Farel, Viret and the young Calvin for the evangelical side.
“able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — the academy of 1537 and its French-speaking ministry.

pos: n. (town and principality on the lake of the same name; the first French-speaking city to receive the Reformation, 1530)
etymology: From French Neuchatel, the new castle, rendering Latin Novum castellum.
biblical_def: Neuchatel has the distinction of being the first French-speaking town to abolish the mass, in November 1530, and it did so under the preaching of William Farel. Farel was no systematician; he was a herald, and he went from market square to market square across the Pays de Vaud and the Jura with a voice that carried and a message that did not vary. Neuchatel became his settled base and his burial place, and it was from there that the French Reformation was pressed outward into Geneva, Lausanne and the Vaud. The town also gave the Reformation one of its most useful instruments, the printing shop of Pierre de Vingle, which issued the Olivetan Bible of 1535 — the first French Bible translated from Hebrew and Greek, and the ancestor of every French Protestant Bible after it. The dictionary records Neuchatel for the plain reason that the gospel travels by heralds and by presses, and this one small town supplied both. “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the logic of the whole mission, and Farel answered it with his feet.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects, tidings as news or account of what has taken place, and to publish as to make known to people in general.
webster_full: PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one that inculcates any thing with earnestness.
TIDINGS, n. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
PUB'LISH, v. To discover or make known to mankind or to people in general; to proclaim; to utter.
GOSPEL, n. The good news of salvation through Jesus Christ; the doctrine of Christ's redemptive work.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
corruption_summary: The first French-speaking town to abolish the mass, 1530; Farel's base, and the press that printed the Olivetan Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a quiet contempt for plain public preaching, which is now widely treated as the crude stage of Christian communication, to be outgrown in favour of conversation, atmosphere, or presence. Farel had nothing but a voice and a text, and with them he opened a language to the gospel.

The principle to recover is that God has appointed proclamation as the means. The commission is to go and speak: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). The chain of necessity runs backward from faith to a sent man: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14). The herald's feet are called beautiful for the sake of his errand — “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7) — and even scattering serves it, for “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).

“went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — de Vingle's press and the Olivetan Bible of 1535.

pos: n. (Swiss town at the lake of Biel, French Bienne; early evangelical, and the parish of Zwingli's teacher Thomas Wyttenbach)
etymology: From German Biel, of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Celtic root for a bend or elbow of water; French Bienne.
biblical_def: Biel is a small town with an outsized place in the history of Reformed doctrine, because of a schoolmaster. Thomas Wyttenbach, a native of Biel, lectured at Basel in 1505 and there taught the young Ulrich Zwingli that indulgences were worthless, that the death of Christ is the sole price of the remission of sins, and that the mass is not a sacrifice; Zwingli said in later years that he had learned these things from Wyttenbach before he had learned them from anyone else. Wyttenbach returned to Biel as its pastor, married in 1524, and carried the town into the Reformation. The dictionary records Biel because the Reformation was not a spontaneous event but a taught one, and the chain of teaching runs back further than the famous names. “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9) describes exactly what happened in that Basel lecture room, and it is the standing reason why the church invests in schoolmasters whose own names the next generation may forget.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines instruction as the act of teaching or informing the understanding, learning as knowledge received by instruction or study, and a master as one who rules or directs.
webster_full: INSTRUC'TION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; information; the act of communicating knowledge.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
MASTER, n. A director; a governor; one who rules or directs; a lord or owner.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university or college, and a common school.
scriptures: Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
Luk 6:40
The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master.
Act 22:3

I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The town of Thomas Wyttenbach, who taught Zwingli at Basel that Christ's death alone remits sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of telling church history as a story of geniuses, which flatters the famous and hides the ordinary labour that produced them. Zwingli is remembered; the man who taught him is not. Biel is the corrective.

The principle to recover is that sound doctrine is handed on by teaching, and that a teacher's work outlives his reputation. Instruction compounds: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning” (Pro 9:9). The scholar is formed by his master — “The disciple is not above his master” (Luk 6:40) — and Paul thought it worth naming the room he was taught in, “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel” (Act 22:3). The office carries the charge: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).

roots_lines: Hebrew musar (H4148) — instruction, discipline, correction that forms; Proverbs 9:9.
Hebrew lamad (H3925) — to teach, to train by repetition; Proverbs 9:9.

“The disciple is not above his master” (Luk 6:40) — Zwingli's own account of where he first learned it.
“For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — Wyttenbach pastor of Biel, and the town reformed.

pos: n. (capital of the Grisons, ancient Rhaetia; reformed under Johannes Comander after the Disputation of 1526)
etymology: From Latin Curia Raetorum, the Roman seat of the Rhaetians; German Chur.
biblical_def: Chur was the bishop's seat of Rhaetia and became the Reformed capital of the Grisons, the loose league of Alpine valleys that governed itself by its own communes. Johannes Comander preached there from 1523, and in January 1526 the League summoned the Disputation of Ilanz, where Comander defended eighteen theses and the assembly resolved that preaching should be from Scripture and that each commune should decide its own worship. The result was a confessional patchwork rather than a uniform settlement, and Chur spent the century defending the evangelical cause in the valleys, sheltering Italian refugees who came over the passes, and — less happily — disciplining the antitrinitarians who came with them. The dictionary records Chur because its method was the right one: not force, but a public hearing with the text as the standard. The Grisons did not always use the standard well, but it set the standard: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines testimony as a solemn declaration made for proving some fact, reason as the faculty distinguishing truth from falsehood, and an elder as one selected to be a ruler or officer.
webster_full: TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
REA'SON, n. A faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, and good from evil.
ELDER, n. One who is older; in Scripture, a person who on account of age is selected to be a ruler or officer.
ANSWER, v.t. To speak in return to a question, call, or argument.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Capital of the Grisons, reformed by Comander and the Disputation of Ilanz, 1526; the text made the standard for the valleys.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern settlement that avoids doctrinal conflict by declaring every position equally private, which is not what the Grisons did. They let each commune decide, but they first made Scripture the public standard by which any decision could be judged and overturned.

The principle to recover is that an appeal to the text is always open and always decisive. The believer is to be equal to the question: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). The ordinary way of settling a disputed matter is an assembly of office-bearers — “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — because one side unanswered always sounds right: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17). The standard itself is fixed: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

roots_lines: Hebrew teudah (H8584) — testimony, attestation, the written witness; Isaiah 8:20.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, the standard appealed to; Isaiah 8:20.
Greek apologia (G627) — a defence, a reasoned answer given on demand; 1 Peter 3:15.

“And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — the League in assembly for the Alpine communes.
“be ready always to give an answer to every man” (1Pe 3:15) — Chur against the antitrinitarians of the passes.

pos: n. (Swiss canton and town; Zwingli's first parish, 1506–1516, and the school of his quarrel with the mercenary trade)
etymology: From German Glarus, through Latin Clarona, from the cell of St Fridolin.
biblical_def: Glarus was Ulrich Zwingli's first charge, and he held it for ten years. The canton supplied soldiers to foreign princes for pay, and Zwingli went with them as chaplain, standing at Novara and at Marignano in 1515, where the Swiss were broken and the young men of his own parish died in heaps for a French quarrel. He came back a declared enemy of the mercenary system, wrote against it in verse and prose, and found that preaching against the pensions cost him the support of the canton's leading families; he left for Einsiedeln in 1516. The dictionary records Glarus because this is where Zwingli learned, before he learned anything else, that the pulpit must speak against the sin the congregation profits by. A ministry that will name every sin except the one that pays is not a ministry. “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24) is the sentence under which Zwingli left his first parish, and it is the sentence under which every faithful pastor eventually loses something.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mercenary as a soldier hired into foreign service, hire as the reward paid for personal service, and mammon as wealth personified as an object of worship rivalling the true God.
webster_full: MER'CENARY, n. One who is hired; a soldier who is hired into foreign service.
HIRE, n. The price, reward or compensation paid for personal service.
MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth personified as an object of worship rivaling the true God.
GAIN, n. Profit; interest; something obtained as an advantage.
scriptures: Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Pro 1:19
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.
He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.
corruption_summary: Zwingli's first parish, and where Marignano taught him to preach against the mercenary pensions his canton lived on.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the pastoral calculation that keeps a congregation's besetting and profitable sin off the preaching list, on the ground that the people are not ready, or that the subject is political, or that the giving would fall. Glarus is the test case, and Zwingli paid the ordinary price for passing it.

The principle to recover is that money is a rival master and must be named as one. The alternative is exclusive, and the Lord states it without remainder: “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). The love of it corrupts doctrine and not merely conduct: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10). It is finally lethal to the men who practise it — “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Pro 1:19) — and it wrecks the household that lives on it: “He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house” (Pro 15:27).

roots_lines: Greek mamonas (G3126) — mammon, riches personified as a master; Matthew 6:24.

“He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house” (Pro 15:27) — Zwingli out of Glarus to Einsiedeln, 1516.

pos: n. (Alsatian city, German Mulhausen; allied to the Swiss Confederation and reformed in 1523)
etymology: From German Mulhausen, the mill houses; French Mulhouse.
biblical_def: Mulhouse stood in Alsace but looked to Switzerland. Having quarrelled with its Habsburg neighbours, the city allied itself with the Swiss cantons in 1515, and that alliance decided its Reformation: the preaching of its own clergy and the influence of Basel, forty miles up the Rhine, carried it to the evangelical side in 1523, and it confirmed the Reformed order in 1529 under the eye of Oecolampadius. For three centuries thereafter it was a Reformed republic inside a Catholic province, an island whose liberty rested entirely on a treaty with men a long way off. The dictionary records Mulhouse as a case study in confessional alliance: a small church can hold a position it could never have defended alone, provided it is genuinely agreed with those it stands beside. “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) is the whole doctrine of such a league in six words, and Mulhouse is what it looks like when the agreement is real.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a league as an alliance between states for mutual aid or defence, unity as the state of being one, and to agree as to be in concord or harmony.
webster_full: LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
U'NITY, n. The state of being one; oneness. Concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
AGREE, v.i. To be in concord or harmony; to live in peace.
BRETHREN, n. pl. Plural of brother; used in the solemn and scriptural style.
scriptures: A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Rom 15:6
That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: An Alsatian city allied to the Swiss, reformed 1523; a Reformed republic inside a Catholic province for three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern alliance built on shared sentiment or shared enemies rather than shared confession, which holds exactly as long as the mood or the enemy lasts. Mulhouse survived because its treaty rested on a settled agreement about the thing itself.

The principle to recover is that real agreement is the condition of real partnership. Scripture states the test as a question that answers itself: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3). Where the agreement is genuine the strength is more than doubled — “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9) — and the end of such union is worship, not advantage: “That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God” (Rom 15:6). The psalmist names the whole state of it: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psa 133:1).

“with one mind and one mouth glorify God” (Rom 15:6) — a Reformed republic inside a Catholic province.

pos: n. (smallest of the Swiss Forest cantons and its town; one of the Five Cantons that stayed with Rome and fought Zurich at Kappel)
etymology: From German Zug, a draught or a pull, from the fishing draught on the lake.
biblical_def: Zug was the least of the inner cantons and the most stubborn. When Zurich reformed, Zug joined Lucerne, Schwyz, Uri and Unterwalden in the Christian Union of 1529 to keep the old religion by arms; its men were in the field at Kappel in October 1531, where Zwingli was killed. Zug then wrote the Reformation out of its own territory and kept it out, and its Landsgemeinde — the open-air assembly of all the men of the canton — voted for the mass with the same voices that had voted for their liberties. The dictionary records Zug for an uncomfortable reason: here the people themselves, freely assembled, chose tradition over the plain text, which disposes of the notion that popular consent is the same thing as truth. “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16) was the call; Zug answered as Jeremiah's hearers did, and the verse itself records that answer: “But they said, We will not walk therein”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canton as a small portion of territory constituting a distinct government, as in Switzerland, tradition as the delivery of doctrines and customs from ancestors to posterity, and a path as a track or course of conduct.
webster_full: CAN'TON, n. A small portion of territory constituting a distinct government, as in Switzerland.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; oral transmission.
PATH, n. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track; a course of life or conduct.
DOCTRINE, n. Principles or positions in any science; whatever is taught; that which is held, put forth as true, and supported by a teacher.
scriptures: Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Mar 7:7
Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: Smallest of the Five Cantons, in arms against Zurich at Kappel 1531; the people themselves voted to keep the mass.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the appeal to inherited practice as though age settled truth — and its mirror image, the appeal to a popular vote as though a majority settled truth. Zug had both: an ancient custom and a free assembly, and together they kept the gospel out of a canton.

The principle to recover is that antiquity and consent are both answerable to the word. Jeremiah's call was to the genuinely old way, which is the written way: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). Where custom has replaced commandment the worship itself is void: “But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9), repeated as “Howbeit in vain do they worship me” (Mar 7:7). And no authority whatever — ancient, popular or angelic — may alter the message: “let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — Kappel, October 1531, and Zwingli dead on the field.
“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — a free assembly that voted to keep the mass.

pos: n. (Swiss city and canton, German Luzern; leader of the Catholic cantons and seat of the papal nuncio after 1579)
etymology: From Latin Lucerna, a lamp, from the monastery of St Leodegar; German Luzern.
biblical_def: Lucerne was the head of the Catholic resistance in Switzerland. It expelled evangelical preachers in the 1520s, took the lead in the Christian Union of 1529, furnished the largest contingent at Kappel, and after the Council of Trent made itself the headquarters of the Counter-Reformation north of the Alps, receiving the permanent papal nuncio in 1579 and the Jesuits in 1574. Its most famous son on the evangelical side, the chronicler and Zwingli's correspondent, had to leave; its most famous churchman, Peter Canisius, worked from Fribourg to undo what Zurich had done. The dictionary records Lucerne because a city can hear the gospel plainly, repeatedly, and from men it knows, and still shut the door — and Scripture names that as a moral act, not an intellectual one. “And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil” (Joh 3:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines light as that which makes objects visible and figuratively spiritual illumination, darkness as the absence of light and figuratively ignorance or sin, and to resist as to withstand or oppose.
webster_full: LIGHT, n. That which makes objects visible; figuratively, knowledge, understanding, or spiritual illumination.
DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; figuratively, ignorance, sin, or spiritual blindness.
RESIST, v.t. To withstand; to oppose; to strive against; to act in opposition to force or authority.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; oral transmission.
scriptures: Joh 3:19
And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.
Act 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Pro 29:1
He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.
And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved.
corruption_summary: Head of the Catholic cantons, chief force at Kappel, and the Counter-Reformation's Swiss capital with the nuncio from 1579.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern instinct to treat every rejection of the gospel as a failure of communication — the wrong tone, the wrong translation, the wrong setting — so that unbelief becomes a problem of method. Lucerne heard it well put, by neighbours, in its own tongue, for a decade.

The principle to recover is that refusal of the light is a judgment on the will. The condemnation is self-incurred: “men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil” (Joh 3:19). Stephen named the same thing as an inherited habit of resistance: “ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye” (Act 7:51). Repeated refusal hardens past remedy — “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy” (Pro 29:1) — and the root is an unwillingness to love what is true: “because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved” (2Th 2:10).
roots_lines: Greek phos (G5457) — light, that which reveals and exposes; John 3:19.
Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness, moral as well as natural; John 3:19.
Greek krisis (G2920) — judgment, the condemnation incurred; John 3:19.
Greek antipipto (G496) — to fall against, to resist; Acts 7:51.
Hebrew oreph (H6203) — the back of the neck, hardened against reproof; Proverbs 29:1.
usage: “men loved darkness rather than light” (Joh 3:19) — evangelical preachers expelled in the 1520s.
“ye do always resist the Holy Ghost” (Act 7:51) — the largest contingent in the field at Kappel.
“hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed” (Pro 29:1) — the Jesuits in 1574, the nuncio in 1579.

pos: n. (Swiss city and canton, French Soleure; its evangelical minority expelled in 1533)
etymology: From Latin Salodurum, a Celtic-Latin name of uncertain sense; German Solothurn.
biblical_def: Solothurn is the Swiss city where the Reformation nearly succeeded and then was driven out. Evangelical preaching gained a substantial following in the 1520s, the two parties came to the edge of civil war in the city in 1533, and when the issue was forced the Catholic majority prevailed; the evangelical minority left for Bern and Basel and the canton remained Catholic, in time becoming a residence of the French ambassadors to the Confederation. Several hundred households went into exile rather than return to the mass. The dictionary records Solothurn because this quiet dispersal, repeated a thousand times across Europe, is how the Reformed churches actually grew: people walked out of a city with what they could carry, and the congregations that received them were enlarged by the loss. “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:10) was addressed to exactly such people, and so was the permission to go: “when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the infliction of pain or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed, exile as the state of being banished, and to banish as to compel a person to leave his own country.
webster_full: PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
EXILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country; the person banished.
BAN'ISH, v.t. To compel a person to leave his own country; to drive away.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
scriptures: But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
Act 8:1

And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: A Swiss city on the edge of civil war in 1533; the evangelical minority left for Bern and Basel rather than return to the mass.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that staying put is always the braver course, so that a believer who moves house for the sake of worship is thought to have given up. Scripture gives express leave to go, and the Reformation was carried across Europe largely by people who took it.

The principle to recover is that flight for conscience is obedience and not cowardice. The Lord Himself authorised it: “But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23). The first great scattering was the church's first great expansion — “there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1). The wanderers are not the discards but the honoured: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38). And the beatitude is spoken straight to them: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10).
roots_summary: Greek dioko (G1377), to persecute; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad.
roots_lines: Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; Matthew 10:23.
Greek pheugo (G5343) — to flee, to take flight; Matthew 10:23.
Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad as seed; Acts 8:1.
Greek diogmos (G1375) — persecution as a settled campaign; Acts 8:1.
Hebrew golah (H1473) — exiles, a company gone into banishment; compare Jeremiah 29:4.
usage: “flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23) — several hundred households out of Solothurn, 1533.
“they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1) — Bern and Basel enlarged by the city's loss.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — a canton kept Catholic by the departure of its best.

pos: n. (Swiss canton divided in 1597 into Reformed Outer Rhodes and Catholic Inner Rhodes)
etymology: From Latin abbatis cella, the abbot's cell, of the abbey of St Gallen; German Appenzell.
biblical_def: Appenzell is the one Swiss canton that solved its religious division by dividing itself. Reformed preaching took the outer, weaving parishes while the inner, pastoral valleys held to Rome, and after seventy years of quarrels over the mass, the monasteries and the pulpits, the canton split in 1597 into Ausserrhoden, Reformed, and Innerrhoden, Catholic, each with its own assembly, each keeping the name. The settlement kept the peace for three centuries and is still on the map. The dictionary records Appenzell because the case is genuinely hard and the lesson is double-edged: a formal separation can be the honest end of an irreconcilable difference, and it can also be the institutionalising of a wound. Scripture does not applaud division — “that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — yet it also requires separation where doctrine is at stake, and commands the church to “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17). Appenzell is where both sentences had to be held at once.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines schism as a division or separation in church affairs and a breach of unity, division as the act of dividing or a part separated from the rest, and concord as union in opinions and interests.
webster_full: SCHISM, n. In church affairs, a division or separation; a breach of unity among people of the same religious faith.
DIVISION, n. The act of dividing; a part separated from the rest; a portion; a section.
CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation.
scriptures: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand:
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
corruption_summary: The canton that divided itself in 1597, Reformed Outer Rhodes and Catholic Inner Rhodes, and kept the peace for three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in both directions. One error calls every separation sinful and so keeps contradictory doctrines yoked together in one body until neither is taught. The other treats separation as costless, so that a congregation divides over preference and calls it conscience.

The principle to recover is that unity is commanded and so is doctrinal separation, and the two are reconciled only by the word. The command is plain: “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10), and the church is to be “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). But the ground of separation is equally plain, and it is doctrine: “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17). The warning against a house at war with itself stands over both parties: “every city or house divided against itself shall not stand” (Mat 12:25).
roots_summary: Greek schisma (G4978), a rent or division; Greek henotes (G1775), unity.
roots_lines: Greek schisma (G4978) — a rent, a tear, a division in a body; 1 Corinthians 1:10.
Greek dichostasia (G1370) — a standing apart, dissension; Romans 16:17.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — a stumbling-block, an offence; Romans 16:17.
Greek henotes (G1775) — oneness, unity to be kept; Ephesians 4:3.
Greek eirene (G1515) — peace, the bond in which unity is kept; Ephesians 4:3.
usage: “that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — seventy years of quarrel over the mass and the pulpits.
“mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine” (Rom 16:17) — the division of 1597 into Outer and Inner Rhodes.
“Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — three centuries of peace on a divided map.
